console.title: Radix Console — Developer tools
console.description: Send tokens and NFTs, create resources, deploy packages, send raw manifests, configure metadata and convert Olympia addresses on the Radix Network.

console.heroDescription: The developer console for the Radix Network. Send tokens and NFTs, create fungible and non-fungible resources, deploy Scrypto packages, send raw transaction manifests, configure on-ledger metadata and convert Olympia addresses. Connect your wallet to start building.

sign-collection.title: Signing Collection
sign-collection.description: Create and manage the Radix Seal collection where your signatures and invitations live, plus the issuer identity everyone receiving them sees.

sign-document.title: Sign Document
sign-document.description: Sign a file with your Radix wallet, off-chain or anchored on-ledger as a soulbound NFT. The file is hashed locally and never uploaded.

guide.guideDescription: Sign documents with your Radix wallet without the file ever leaving your browser: only its Blake2b-256 hash is signed. You can sign alone, sign with several people by passing a JSON certificate around off-chain, or sign with several people on the ledger with the Radix Seal flow, where every signature is recorded as an NFT and anyone can verify it by reading the network, without depending on this site. The ledger flow involves four NFTs with distinct roles: the Seal (your insignia), your signing collection (your personal archive), invitations (notices of who is asked to sign) and signatures (the record that actually counts). The glossary below explains each one and how verification works.
guideSteps: 1. One-time setup for the ledger flow: mint your Seal (non-transferable insignia, once) and create your signing collection, optionally with your company identity (name, website and logo get recorded into its metadata).

2. Drop the document. It is hashed locally and never uploaded; its Blake2b-256 hash appears under the box. If the PDF carries embedded Radix data (certificate, original or request), it is broken down right there.

3. Sign alone: choose what identity to disclose and the output format (.radixsig.json certificate or PDF with the certificate embedded) and press Sign. Optionally anchor the hash as a soulbound NFT in your collection.

4. Create the request: one invitation NFT per signer, valid for that document only, is minted and deposited into each signer's wallet. With "Sign and send", your own signature NFT is minted in the same transaction.

5. Share the link: it carries the right network, the document name and the output formats you chose. If you keep the tab open, the document travels on its own, browser to browser, over an encrypted direct channel. You can also download the PDF with the request embedded and send just that file.

6. Each signer opens the link, receives or uploads the document, the tool checks it matches the request's hash, and they sign from their wallet by minting their signature NFT. On their first time, their Seal and collection are set up on the spot.
7. Status refreshes automatically every 30 seconds by reading the ledger: who has signed and who is pending. Once complete, you download the certificate or the signed PDF.

8. Verify: in the Verify tab you can drop the file with its certificate, a self-contained signed PDF, or paste the request key (collection + id) to read the signatures straight from the ledger, with no certificate and no wallet.

glossary.definition: A non-transferable NFT you mint once from the official Radix Seal resource. It has two jobs: it identifies you as a signer and it is the only key able to mint into your signing collection. It can never be sold, moved or burned. Without your Seal nobody, not even this site, can create anything in your name.

Your personal, reusable NFT resource, created once. Its owner rule is locked forever and requires your Seal. Inside it, with consecutive numbering (#1, #2, #3...), the other two NFT types are minted: the invitations you issue and your signatures. Everything inside is non-transferable and its data can never be edited. It works as your own self-custodied certificate authority: you issue, the ledger attests.

Minted by the request issuer, one per required signer, into their own collection, and deposited into each invitee's wallet. It carries the document hash, the invited account, the total signer count and the id of the batch's first invitation; thanks to that, the full batch is the public, immutable list of who must sign, readable from the request key alone. It is a notice, not a signature: the issuer can recall it after a wrong address, but can never touch a signature.

Minted by each signer into their own collection at the moment of signing. It carries the document hash, the signer's account, the key of the request it answers and the date. This is the record that counts as the signature: non-transferable, data locked, and impossible to forge because only the signer's Seal can mint into their collection.

The certificate holds one ROLA proof per signer: the wallet signs a challenge derived from the document hash and the canonical metadata. Verification re-hashes the file, rebuilds the challenge and validates each cryptographic signature against its account's public key. If a single byte of the document changes, the hash no longer matches and verification fails.

A signer only counts as signed if the chain of custody read from the ledger holds: a signature NFT with the document's hash exists inside a collection whose owner rule, locked forever, requires one specific Seal, and that non-transferable Seal sits in the signer's account. Pending signers are the invitees of the batch for which that check finds no signature NFT yet.

The signature proves account control, document integrity and date; the disclosed name is self-declared by the wallet. It is not a qualified electronic signature (eIDAS QES) because no authority binds the account to a verified legal identity.

chat.title: Secure Chat
chat.description: End-to-end encrypted chat between browsers. Both sides prove their identity with a Radix wallet signature, verified locally, and no server can read or impersonate.

guide.guideDescription: A direct, end-to-end encrypted conversation between two browsers. Each participant signs a challenge with their Radix Wallet that commits to a fresh ephemeral key; both proofs are verified locally (signature + account derivation), and the session key is agreed from that verified exchange. Messages travel over WebRTC with an extra AES-256-GCM layer and anti-replay sequence numbers, and the signaling server only relays the connection handshake and can read nothing.
guideSteps: 1. Connect your wallet and press Create secure chat; sign the room challenge.
2. Send the generated link or QR code to the other person over any channel.
3. When they open it, connect their wallet and sign, both identities are verified and the room turns secure.
4. The header shows the other side's wallet-verified account address, so you know who you are really talking to.
5. Chat freely; messages exist only in the two browsers. Leaving the page ends the conversation and nothing is stored.

glossary.definition: Each peer's ROLA signature is checked in your browser: the Ed25519 signature must be valid and the public key must derive to the claimed account address. A failed check closes the room.

Ephemeral ECDH keys are exchanged inside the signed challenges, so the derived AES-256-GCM key belongs to this conversation only (forward secrecy: it never existed before and is destroyed when the page closes).
Every message is sealed with its sequence number and sender role; replayed, reordered or reflected messages fail authentication and close the room.

encrypt-document.title: Encrypt Document
encrypt-document.description: Encrypt any file with your Radix wallet signature and share it peer-to-peer over an encrypted channel. The file never leaves your browser.

guide.guideDescription: Encrypts files with a key derived from a deterministic Radix Wallet signature: only the account that encrypted a file can ever unlock it, from any device, with no key stored anywhere. Files are processed in chunks in your browser (no size limit), kept in local browser storage and shared directly between browsers over an end-to-end encrypted WebRTC channel. No server ever sees a byte of your file. There are two encryption methods: ROLA only, where you decide who to release the key to, and ROLA + Ledger, where the encryptor always mints a signature NFT recording that this account encrypted the file and, optionally, one invitation NFT per authorized receiver, leaving a public record of who encrypted the file and who may decrypt it.
guideSteps: 1. Pick the method. ROLA only: the key is derived from your signature and you release decryption to whoever you approve. ROLA + Ledger: you also authorize specific accounts on the ledger, so only they can request decryption from you.

2. Setup (ROLA + Ledger only, one time): you need your Seal NFT and your signing collection, the same ones Sign Document uses. If they are missing, the boxes to deploy and create them appear before you can encrypt.

3. Encrypt: connect your wallet, drop any file and press Encrypt. For ROLA + Ledger you first add the list of authorized receivers. Your wallet signs a challenge unique to this file and the AES-256 key is derived from that signature. For ROLA + Ledger, a second confirmation mints your encryption signature NFT (the record that this account encrypted the file) plus one invitation NFT per authorized receiver, deposited into their accounts. Receivers are optional: with none, only your signature NFT is minted.

4. Download or share: save the .radixseal.enc container, or press Share to get a link and QR code for the receiver. The file travels browser-to-browser when the receiver opens the link; keep this tab open.
5. Approve (ROLA only): when the receiver asks to decrypt, you'll see who is asking and for which file (check the fingerprint), and sign in your wallet to release the key.

6. Approve (ROLA + Ledger): the receiver signs a ROLA challenge with their invited account when requesting decryption. Your browser checks on the ledger that this account holds the file's invitation NFT before showing you the request; you'll see their proven account and the verified-invitation badge.

7. Reverse flow: if you received a .radixseal.enc file, open the Decrypt tab, load it and request decryption. The tool detects the file's method: for ROLA + Ledger you must connect the invited account and sign the challenge.
8. Sender shortcut: if the connected wallet is the account that encrypted the file, the Decrypt tab unlocks it directly, no link needed.

9. Receipt (ROLA + Ledger, optional): after decrypting, the receiver can mint a receipt NFT into their collection as public, permanent evidence that they obtained the key, verifiable by the sender on the ledger.

glossary.definition: Radix Off-Ledger Authentication: the wallet signs a challenge to prove account ownership. Ed25519 signatures are deterministic, so the same account over the same challenge always re-creates the same encryption key.

ROLA only binds the key to your account and you decide who to approve for decryption, leaving no on-chain trace. ROLA + Ledger adds a verifiable permission layer: you authorize specific accounts in advance with an invitation NFT, and both the permission and the decryption become checkable on the ledger.

In ROLA + Ledger, the encryptor always mints this into their own collection: a public, permanent record that this account encrypted the file (its container header hash). It is the encryption counterpart of a document signature, minted whether or not there are authorized receivers.

In ROLA + Ledger, the sender mints one invitation per authorized receiver into their signing collection and deposits it into each receiver's wallet. It carries the container hash and the authorized account. Only accounts holding this invitation can send the ROLA challenge to request decryption. Receivers are optional.

The ROLA challenge the receiver signs to request the key. It is bound to the exact container hash, the session room and the network, so a captured signature cannot be reused in another session or for another file.

An optional record the receiver mints into their own collection after obtaining the key. It is non-transferable with locked data: public, permanent evidence that this account decrypted the file, verifiable by anyone on the ledger.

The encrypted container. Its header keeps the original file name, the encrypting account, network, site and protection method (ROLA or ROLA + Ledger) visible so decryption can be routed; the content is AES-256-GCM encrypted per chunk.

The key is bound to the encrypting account, this site (origin), its dApp definition and the network. Files encrypted elsewhere (for example on localhost) cannot be unlocked here, and the tool reports this explicitly.
Direct browser-to-browser channel, encrypted end-to-end (DTLS). A signaling room is used only to exchange the connection handshake, never file data or keys.

claim-package-royalties.title: Claim Package Royalties
claim-package-royalties.description: Claim accumulated XRD royalties from a Scrypto package.

guide.guideDescription: Scrypto packages can configure royalties: a small amount of XRD that accrues every time someone calls their blueprints. This tool builds the transaction that claims that accumulated balance and deposits it into your account. You must hold the package owner badge — the network rejects claims from any other account.
guideSteps: 1. Connect the wallet that holds the package owner badge.
2. Paste the address of the package (package_…) whose royalties you want to claim.
3. Select the account to deposit the claimed XRD into.
4. Simulate the transaction to see the accrued amount before signing.
5. Press Claim and approve the transaction in your wallet.

glossary.definition: An XRD fee defined by a blueprint's author, charged automatically on every invocation and accumulated in the package itself until its owner claims it.
The NFT you received when deploying the package. The claim instruction presents that badge as proof; without it, the transaction fails.

send-transaction.title: Send Transaction
send-transaction.description: Build a transfer of tokens and NFTs to one or several accounts with the wallet transaction builder, and inspect the generated manifest.

guide.guideDescription: The definitive tool for asset transfer on the Radix network. Unlike traditional transactions on Ethereum or Bitcoin, on Radix you can transfer multiple tokens and NFTs to multiple recipients within a single transaction, ensuring that either all transfers succeed, or none do (atomicity). Ideal for mass payments, airdrops, or simply reorganizing your own funds across accounts.
guideSteps: 1. Source of funds: On the main panel, select the account from which resources will be extracted. Ensure this account has sufficient balance.
2. Add Recipients: Click 'Add transfer' to create a sending block. You can add as many blocks as you need for different recipients.
3. Configure each transfer: In each block, paste the exact address of the recipient (ensure it starts with 'account_...').
4. Resource selection: Choose which token or NFT you want to send. If sending NFTs, you must select exactly which unique identifiers (IDs) will be transferred.
5. Amounts: Enter the exact token amount to send. The system will automatically validate that you don't exceed your available balance.
6. Add Proofs (Optional): If the recipient is a smart component that demands special identification (Badge), click 'Add proof' and select the credential NFT.
7. Simulation (Critical step): Always click 'Simulate transaction'. This will virtually execute the transaction on the network without spending funds, showing you exactly what will happen.
8. Final submission: If the simulation is green, click 'Send transaction'. Your Radix Wallet will pop up asking you to review and cryptographically sign the order.

glossary.definition: Property guaranteeing that a transaction involving multiple transfers either executes fully or fails completely; it will never remain half-done.
A type of token (usually an NFT) serving as a digital access key. It proves you have permission to perform a specific action.
Mass distribution of tokens or NFTs to multiple wallet addresses, usually for free or as a reward.

create-token.title: Create Token
create-token.description: Create a fungible or non-fungible resource with custom metadata, supply and behaviour, and deploy it to the Radix Network.

guide.guideDescription: Become the creator of your own economy. Radix treats tokens as first-class citizens on the network, meaning you don't need to write complex smart contracts to create a secure and standard token. This graphical interface builds the exact manifest to instantiate (mint) both Fungible and Non-Fungible resources with advanced business rules and persistent ledger metadata.
guideSteps: 1. Account Selection: Choose the account that will pay network fees and, by default, receive the initial supply of the created resources.
2. Asset Type: Select 'Fungible' if creating a cryptocurrency, loyalty points, or shares (all units are equal). Select 'Non-Fungible' for digital art, event tickets, or unique certificates.

3. Project Identity (Metadata): Fill in the fields users will see in their wallets. 'Name' and 'Symbol' (e.g., BTC) are crucial. 'Icon URL' should be a direct link to an internet-hosted image (preferably square).
4. Initial Supply: Decide how many units will be generated upon creation. If you set 0, the token will be born with no circulation.
5. Divisibility (Fungibles only): Indicate how many fractions a unit can be divided into. The standard is 18 decimals. If it represents whole objects (e.g., 'Cars'), set divisibility to 0.
6. Owner Role: Decide who will have administrative authority over the token in the future. You can assign it to 'None' (forever immutable), 'Anyone', or demand a specific 'Badge'.
7. Simulation & Deployment: Simulate the transaction to verify the network accepts the config, then send it to your wallet for signing.

glossary.definition: Identical, mutually interchangeable assets, like regular money or Bitcoin. One 10-dollar bill is worth the same as another 10-dollar bill.
A unique, unrepeatable digital asset. Each NFT has its own identifier, like an original painting or a specific theater seat.
The public, decentralized Radix network accounting book where your token creation is permanently recorded.
The number of decimal places a token can have. With 18 decimals (maximum), you could send 0.000000000000000001 of a token.

my-resources.title: My Resources
my-resources.description: Manage the tokens you control: mint more units or NFTs, burn, lock metadata, change the owner role, recall and freeze vaults.

guide.guideDescription: The master admin dashboard for token creators. This tool is designed exclusively for you to manage resources over which you retain administrative privileges (Owner Role). It allows you to execute token lifecycle actions configured as 'Updatable' during creation.
guideSteps: 1. Browse inventory: Select the account holding your token 'Badges' (master keys). The tool automatically scans the network for resources you control.
2. Select Resource: Click the token or NFT you wish to administer from the list.
3. Choose Action: Depending on token creation settings, you'll see options: 'Mint' (create new supply), 'Burn' (destroy existing tokens), 'Modify Metadata', or 'Freeze' vaults.
4. Authorization (Provide Badge): Network rules demand proof of authority. The interface will try to auto-attach the required Badge from your account. If the Badge is elsewhere, transfer it first.
5. Fill Parameters: If you chose 'Mint Fungibles', enter the print amount. If modifying metadata, enter new values.
6. Confirm changes: Always use the 'Simulate' function to ensure the admin action doesn't violate business rules, then send the order to your Radix Wallet.

glossary.definition: The process of creating new units of an existing token, increasing its total circulating supply.
The permanent and irreversible destruction of tokens, removing them from circulation forever.
A drastic compliance/legal action locking a specific account, temporarily preventing it from sending or receiving that particular token.

build-manifest.title: Build Manifest
build-manifest.description: Build manifests visually using templates or interactive blocks with real-time code and flow previews.

guide.guideDescription: A revolutionary tool democratizing the Radix transaction language (RTML). Radix uses 'Manifests', text scripts describing exactly what occurs in a transaction. This visual interface lets you stack logic blocks (like Lego bricks) to build hyper-advanced transaction logic without writing a single line of code.
guideSteps: 1. Choose a Starting Point: Start with a blank canvas or use the 'Templates' dropdown for common structures (like 'Simple Send' or 'Swap').
2. Add Blocks: Search the left panel for the instruction type needed. E.g., drag 'Withdraw' to pull funds from an account, or 'Deposit' to insert them.
3. Connect Logic: In Radix, extracted resources are temporarily held in the 'Worktop'. Ensure actions follow logical order: first withdraw to Worktop, then deposit from Worktop to destination.
4. Adjust Parameters: Click each block to configure. Enter correct addresses (accounts, components), numeric amounts, and resource identifiers.
5. Monitor Code: As you add blocks, watch the right 'Preview' panel. The tool writes raw Manifest code in real-time, helping you learn native syntax.
6. Execution: Run a simulation and send the finalized transaction to the wallet.

glossary.definition: A human-readable text file describing exact transaction intent step-by-step, designed for user auditing before signing.
Temporary transaction memory. Withdrawn tokens drop onto the Worktop. If tokens remain on the Worktop when the transaction ends, safety protocols will abort the transaction.
An individual command within the manifest, like calling a function, moving an asset, or creating a proof.

deploy-package.title: Deploy Package
deploy-package.description: Deploy a new blueprint package to the network by attaching your WASM and RPD files and submitting a transaction with your Radix Wallet.

guide.guideDescription: The bridge between your local development environment and the Radix network. A 'Package' in Radix equals a Smart Contract in Ethereum, but written in Scrypto and compiled to WebAssembly. This tool handles packaging, signing, and immutably publishing your code on the global ledger.
guideSteps: 1. Local Compilation: Ensure you've run `scrypto build` locally on your project code. This generates two essential files in the `/target/...` folder.
2. Funding Account: Select the wallet account that will pay the XRD upload fees. (Uploading code costs computational power).
3. WASM File: Upload the `.wasm` file. This is the brain of your contract, the compiled and obfuscated logic code.
4. RPD File: Upload the associated `.rpd` (Radix Package Definition) file. It's a map explaining to the network how to read the WASM, its methods, and utilized resources.
5. Global Permissions: Optionally configure future package upgradeability. By default, packages are immutable to guarantee user trust.
6. Deployment Transaction: Simulate and send. Once confirmed, you'll receive the final address of your package (`package_...`), used to instantiate components.

glossary.definition: Radix's native programming language, based on Rust, exclusively specialized in decentralized finance and secure asset handling.
A highly optimized, ultra-fast binary code format the Radix network executes directly in its virtual machine.
The 'building plans' within the package. They define the generic structure users will subsequently instantiate.
The final container holding one or more Blueprints and executable code. It possesses a fixed network address.

transaction-manifest.title: Transaction Manifest
transaction-manifest.description: Write a raw transaction manifest and send it as a transaction request to your Radix Wallet.

guide.guideDescription: The most powerful (and dangerous) tool for advanced users and veteran developers. A raw text console accepting RTML code directly. Bypasses graphical interfaces, allowing surgical network manipulation via assertions and complex conditional logic.
guideSteps: 1. Code Editor: Write your manifest directly in the interactive terminal. The console features basic syntax highlighting for readability.
2. Network Context: Verify in the top right corner you're targeting the correct network (Mainnet for real, Stokenet for testing).
3. Blob Handling: If your transaction requires uploading large binaries or weird data (like massive state initialization), add 'Blobs' in the auxiliary interface.
4. Strict Validation: Click 'Simulate transaction'. The network parses the text for typos, non-existent addresses, or insufficient funds.
5. Execution: Send to the wallet. Being a raw manifest, the Radix Wallet interprets the text to display a visual summary of your code's intent.

glossary.definition: Radix Transaction Manifest Language. The secure scripting language orchestrating smart contract calls on Radix.
Binary Large Object. Hexadecimal encoded data packages attached to transactions without cluttering main manifest text.
Manifest security instructions instantly aborting the entire transaction if conditions aren't met (e.g., 'Cancel all if price drops below X').

component-panel.title: Component Panel
component-panel.description: Read the blueprint of any on-ledger component live from the network and get an instant control panel to execute its public methods.

guide.guideDescription: A direct window into live network state. Unlike other networks demanding full web DApp builds to interact with smart contracts, Radix exposes contracts (Components) natively. This tool reads technical definitions of any component, auto-generating buttons and forms for immediate interaction.
guideSteps: 1. Locate Component: Paste the full address of a live component (usually starting with `component_...`).
2. Blueprint Analysis: The tool scans the origin package, displaying a table with technical data (origin package, base blueprint name).
3. Explore Methods: You'll see a list of 'Public Methods' (functions left open by the developer). Select one to execute.
4. Fill Arguments: If the function requires data (like 'amount to swap' or 'user ID'), the interface generates specific input fields.
5. Capture Returns: If the function spits resources back (e.g., buying returns an NFT), you must select a 'Destination' account in your wallet. Otherwise, the transaction fails to protect your funds!
6. Confirm: Simulate interaction and sign.

glossary.definition: The 'live' version of a Blueprint. If the Blueprint is the technical plan, the Component is the actual building operating on the network.
A programmed specific action within the component. A vending machine might have methods like 'insert_coin' or 'select_soda'.
Using a static Blueprint to create a new operational Component on the network with independent memory and state.

configure-metadata.title: Configure Metadata
configure-metadata.description: Inspect and update the on-ledger metadata of accounts, resources, components and validators.

guide.guideDescription: The ultimate dashboard to maintain your creations' public identity. Everything on Radix (accounts, tokens, contracts, validators) has a reserved network space for 'Metadata'. This tool allows inspection and alteration of this data, like updating token imagery or changing DApp descriptions.
guideSteps: 1. Owner: Select the account presenting administrative credentials. Modifying public data requires authority.
2. Target Entity: Enter the exact address of the modification target (an account, a `resource_...`, or a package).
3. Inspection: The tool fetches current metadata directly from the network.
4. Modification: Use '+' buttons to add fields or edit existing ones. You can change names, descriptions, image URLs, and search tags.
5. Confirm: Run simulation. The network instantly checks if the owner account has adequate permissions, then forwards to wallet.

glossary.definition: Information attached to an element describing its properties (the digital 'ID card' of the asset). Affects visual presentation, not mathematical logic.
Generic term covering anything global on the Radix network with an address, like components, packages, or resources.
Keywords associated with an asset allowing community web explorers to index and classify it.

convert-olympia-address.title: Convert Olympia Address
convert-olympia-address.description: Convert an Olympia address into its Babylon equivalent (and back), and generate the QR to import the account into the Radix Wallet app.

guide.guideDescription: A vital historical tool. Radix underwent a massive global tech upgrade (from the 'Olympia' network to the current 'Babylon' network). Addresses changed formats. This utility translates old addresses to the new format (and legacy Babylon accounts back to their Olympia address), and builds the same import QR the Olympia Desktop Wallet shows for migrating accounts into the mobile Radix Wallet.
guideSteps: 1. Identify Old Address: Obtain the old address requiring modernization (old accounts started with `rdx1...`, old resources by common Olympia token names). You can also paste a legacy Babylon account (`account_...`) to recover its original Olympia address.
2. Input Data: Paste into the text field.
3. Instant Conversion: The tool derives the corresponding Babylon address (the reverse direction recovers the public key from an on-ledger signature).
4. Copy Result: Use the copy button to utilize the new `account_...` address on the current network.

5. Import into the Wallet: For account addresses, adjust the account type, address index and seed phrase length, then scan the generated QR with the Radix Wallet app (Settings → Troubleshooting → Import from a Legacy Wallet) following the on-screen steps.

glossary.definition: Version 1.0 of the Radix mainnet. Operated flawlessly until its planned upgrade, but featured less scalable contract tech.
The current hyper-advanced Radix network version, featuring full Scrypto environment integration and universal smart accounts.
Mathematical process taking a base address and, using predictable rules, generating an entirely different but mathematically linked address.

sbor-decoder.title: SBOR Encoder / Decoder
sbor-decoder.description: Paste any hex-encoded SBOR payload (state, events, schemas) and read it decoded, human-readable.

guide.guideDescription: Low-level forensic tool. The Radix network compresses all its data (like contract states or emitted events) into an incomprehensible binary format called SBOR to save massive storage space. This console translates that machine language into readable text, and vice versa.
guideSteps: 1. Locate Source Code: Get the long hexadecimal string you wish to understand (usually extracted from network explorers during deep transaction searches).
2. Paste Payload: Insert the hex string into the main field.
3. Automatic Analysis: The tool attempts instant decompression and parsing of the string.
4. Tree View: Explore the result in a hierarchical panel breaking down exactly how Radix understood the internal data (arrays, maps, structs, numeric types).
5. Encoding (Advanced): You can write structured JSON text and use the tool in reverse to generate the compressed SBOR binary.

glossary.definition: Scrypto Binary Object Representation. Radix's extremely efficient data packaging method ensuring light-speed network travel and storage.
Numeric system including numbers and letters A through F. Used in computing as shorthand for extremely long binary strings.
The 'useful cargo' of a message. In a payment instruction, the payload is the money amount, stripped of cryptographic bureaucracy.

address-book.title: Address Book
address-book.description: Save and organise Radix addresses (accounts, validators, pools, components and packages) by category, verified on-ledger. The same address book as in your wallet profile.

address-utils.title: Address Utilities
address-utils.description: Inspect and validate any Radix address, derive accounts from public keys and browse the well-known network addresses.

guide.guideDescription: The network address 'DNA analyzer'. In Radix, an element's address (the long text starting with account_ or resource_) contains hidden technical information. This tool decrypts the address, detailing exactly what it is, its native network, and the entity it belongs to.
guideSteps: 1. Inspection Mode: Paste any Radix address. The tool dismantles it, informing if it belongs to Mainnet/Stokenet, if it's a resource, component, or package, and its encoding (Bech32m).
2. Known Addresses: Click the side panel to list foundational system pillars pre-installed at network zero (XRD token, Secp256k1 token, Consensus component, etc.).

3. Cryptographic Derivation: (Advanced) Select the top derivation tab. Enter a raw cryptographic 'Public Key' and select its curve (Ed25519 for Radix users, Secp256k1 for Ethereum/Bitcoin exports). The tool creates the virtual Radix account tied to that key.

glossary.definition: Your cryptographic ID number, safely shareable with everyone. Your addresses are generated from this key.
Ultra-secure cryptographic algorithms. Radix uses the former for modern speed, while Bitcoin/Ethereum popularized the latter.
The global standard text formatting Radix (and Bitcoin) uses for addresses. Mathematically designed to prevent human confusion reading letters like lowercase 'O' or zero '0'.

faucet.title: Test Faucet
faucet.description: Fund a Stokenet account with 10,000 test XRD in one click, straight from the network faucet.

guide.guideDescription: The infinite development bank. A Faucet dispenses free, zero-value tokens enabling you to test projects, make mistakes, and build apps on the test network (Stokenet) without risking real fees.
guideSteps: 1. Network Verification: Ensure the 'Stokenet' network is active (top right corner). The Faucet does not, and will never, function on the real network (Mainnet).
2. Receiving Account: Use the dropdown to select which test account will receive free funds.

3. Direct Execution: Press the main button. Unlike other tools, this silently interacts with the official RadixDlt Faucet server, instantly delivering 10,000 test XRD and batches of other simulated tokens.
4. Abuse Limits: The Faucet detects your account and temporarily blocks you if used more than once per 'Epoch' (a network time measure lasting approx. 30-60 minutes).

glossary.definition: An automatic, charitable system gifting zero-value cryptocurrency to developers to encourage technical DApp experimentation.
Radix's harmless twin brother. A fully functioning network where all money is fake, and history occasionally resets.
A geological time phase within the Radix network. At each Epoch's start, consensus servers rotate and background accounting tasks execute.

wallet-playground.title: Wallet Playground
wallet-playground.description: Experiment with Radix Wallet data requests: ask for accounts with ownership proofs and verify them with ROLA, like a real dApp.

guide.guideDescription: The ultimate simulation tool for Front-End and Web3 developers. This utility lets you act as a 'customs agent', attempting to request private user data from the connected wallet exactly as a real DApp (like an exchange or web3 game) would.
guideSteps: 1. Request Mode: Select the desired intrusion level. Request simple 'Accounts' (knowing where to charge/pay), escalate to 'Persona' (abstract identity), or even private data like linked Emails/Phones.
2. Authentication Parameters: Decide if requested accounts/data must be accompanied by strict cryptographic proof (ROLA), demanding the user's phone sign an unmistakable digital declaration.
3. Send Request (Dapp-to-Wallet): Click 'Send Request'. Watch your mobile phone; the native Radix Connect system interface will pop up asking end-user permission.

4. Response Analysis: Approve the request on your phone. Your computer's console will print the security JSON packet returned by the wallet, allowing you to program your DApp based on real structures.

glossary.definition: A security standard where the wallet proves account ownership without making a financial network transaction; akin to showing an ID card instead of paying with a bank card.
A conventional web application holding direct, two-way communication capabilities with cryptocurrency networks and smart contracts, bypassing intermediary servers.
A Radix Wallet exclusive concept. An abstract mobile identity (e.g., 'Business Profile' or 'Gamer Profile') linking specific accounts without exposing your entire wealth.

staking.title: Staking
staking.description: Manage the staking of your accounts: stake, unstake and claim on your validators with individual, batch or mixed actions — the same panel the wallet profile uses.

guide.guideDescription: Full XRD staking panel. Delegate to one or several validators, unstake and claim your unlocked XRD. Supports global batch actions (split an amount across validators), cart mode to combine different operations into a single transaction, and owner mode for validators you control.
guideSteps: 1. Account: pick the account whose staking position you want to manage.
2. Validators: you get one row per validator you already stake with; use the search to add new validators.
3. Individual action: on each row enter an amount and choose Stake, Unstake or Claim.
4. Global action: enter an amount at the top and it is split equally across the selected validators.
5. Cart mode: configure several operations on different rows and they are grouped into a single transaction.
6. Send: press "Send to wallet" and sign the transaction in your Radix Wallet.

glossary.definition: Liquid Stake Units: the token you receive when staking, representing your share in the validator.
When unstaking you receive an NFT redeemable for XRD once the waiting period ends.
Special view for validators you control: shows the owner locked stake and its unlocks.

mcp.title: MCP Server
mcp.description: Connect AI assistants (Claude Code, Antigravity, Cursor, …) to this site: search the docs, inspect any ledger address and prepare transaction manifests through the Model Context Protocol.

guide.guideDescription: The bridge between AI assistants and Radix. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard that lets AI tools use external services. This page gives your AI everything the site offers: documentation search, ledger data for accounts, components, packages and validators, and every console action as ready-to-sign transaction manifests.
guideSteps: 1. Pick your AI client: select Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, Antigravity or Gemini CLI and copy the install snippet.
2. Connect: paste the snippet in the client's terminal or configuration file. No API key is required.
3. Optional skill file: download the SKILL.md and drop it into your agent's skills folder so it knows every workflow of this server.
4. Ask away: the AI can now answer questions from the docs, inspect any address or transaction, list validators, and build token/staking/transfer manifests.
5. Sign safely: MCP never touches your funds. Any transaction the AI prepares must be pasted in the Transaction Manifest tool and signed with your own wallet.

olympia.stepsTitle: How to import the account in the Radix Wallet (Android & iOS)
steps: Install and set up the Radix Wallet app on your phone (Google Play / App Store).
Keep the Olympia Desktop Wallet seed phrase at hand (or your Ledger device and the Radix Connector browser extension for hardware accounts).
In the app, open Settings (gear icon) → Troubleshooting → "Import from a Legacy Wallet".
Scan the QR code shown above.
Review the account to import — the wallet shows the obsolete Olympia address and the new Babylon address — and tap "Import".
Software account: type the Olympia seed phrase to verify ownership. Ledger account: connect and confirm with your Ledger via Radix Connector.
Done — the account appears in the wallet as "Legacy" with its new Babylon address. Keep the Olympia seed phrase safe; you may still need it.
olympia.stepsNote: The flow is identical on Android and iOS. Account type, address index and seed phrase length must match the original Olympia wallet, otherwise the wallet will reject the verification.

argTypes.Bool: True or false. Write true or false, without quotes.

fields.nftCustomFieldsNote: This resource carries its own fields on its NFTs. In Radix a mint has to supply all of them, so no field is optional: whatever you leave empty is minted empty, but it is still sent. They are listed above in the order its schema fixed. The grey text in each one is the value an existing NFT carries, or its data type with a sample when it carries none. Fields whose type does not fit in a text box (lists, enums) are disabled. If the collection has no NFT yet there is nothing to read the schema from, and only the three standard fields are sent.

connector.title: Sign transactions (local connector)
connector.hint: This server prepares and previews transactions but cannot sign them. Install the local connector to pair your Radix Wallet and sign — your private key never leaves your phone.
connector.how: Signing needs a live channel to your phone, which a stateless web server can't hold. So a small local MCP server, radix-connector-mcp, does it: it opens the Radix Connect channel and your phone approves. Install it once and both servers work together.
connector.installCargoLabel: Option A · with a Rust toolchain (any OS)
connector.installPrebuiltLabel: Option B · prebuilt binary (no Rust needed - recommended option)
connector.registerTitle: 2. Register it with your AI client
connector.registerHint: The local connector is registered under the name "radix-connector". If the binary is not on your PATH, use its absolute path as the command. Reload the client once so the new tools appear.
pairSteps: Ask your AI to call pair_wallet (it will show the QR as an image, ASCII text, or local png file).
Scan the QR in your Radix Wallet. The AI will wait for you.
The AI calls pair_status to finish pairing (once per device).
From then on, it will use send_transaction and you approve on your phone.
connector.hallucinationAlert: ALERT: AI can hallucinate and generate unsolicited transactions. Carefully examine the transaction on your phone before signing, and always run preliminary tests on stokenet.
connector.security: The phone signs every action (you always approve there). The connector only stores the channel password locally; the private key and the QR never leave your machine.

network.title: How does the MCP choose between mainnet and stokenet?
network.body: Every ledger and console tool accepts an optional "network" parameter ("mainnet" or "stokenet") that defaults to mainnet. Just mention the network in your question — "list the validators on stokenet" — and the AI fills the parameter for you. Addresses also carry their network in the prefix: mainnet uses …rdx1 (account_rdx1…) and stokenet uses …tdx_2_1 (account_tdx_2_1…), so the AI can detect the right network with the inspect_address tool and will never mix networks in one transaction.
